This is the cohomology ring of a product of three spheres over $ \mathbb{Q} $, and $ A $ is a graded subring of $ R $, with the same additive lattice as $ R $, i.e., a "graded lattice" in $ R $, and generated by a homogeneous basis of $ R $.

We are asked: **what is the strongest statement that can be proved about the existence of a CW-complex $ X $ such that $ H^*(X; \mathbb{Z}) \cong A $**?

Let’s analyze the options.

---

**Option A**:
> There exists a single $ X $, depending only on $ (d_1, d_2, d_3) $, such that for every $ A $, $ H^*(X; \mathbb{Z}) \cong A $.

This is **too strong**. $ A $ is a subring of $ R $, and different $ A $'s can be different. So a single $ X $, independent of $ A $, can't have cohomology ring isomorphic to all $ A $'s. So A is **not** the best.

---

**Option B**:
> There exists a $ X_A $, whose cohomology is isomorphic to $ A $, provided that $ d_i $ are pairwise distinct.

This is **strong**, but only under a condition (distinct $ d_i $), and it says that for any $ A $, a $ X $ exists with $ H^* \cong A $. But is this always true?

We are not given that $ A $ is a ring of cohomology of a space, only that it is a subring of $ R $, with same lattice. So is $ A $ always a cohomology ring of a space?

**Not necessarily**. So B is **strong**, but not always true.

---

**Option C****:
> There exists a $ X_A $, such that $ H^*(X) \subseteq A $, i.e., $ H^* \cong B \subseteq A $.

This is **weaker** than D, and says that only a subring of $ A $ is realizable as a cohomology ring. So C is **not the best**.

---

**Option D****:
> There exists a $ X_A $, such that $ H^*(X) \cong A $.

This is **strong**, and says that for any $ A $, a space exists with cohomology ring isomorphic to $ A $.

But is this always true?

**No**, in general. Not all rings are realizable as cohomology rings of spaces. So D is **not always true**.

---

**Option E****:
> There exists a $ X_A $, such that $ H^*(X) \mod \text{tors} \cong A $.

This is **weaker than D**, but **stronger than C**. It says that the cohomology ring of a space, after quotienting by torsion, is isomorphic to $ A $.

This is **always true**, in a sense: any ring $ A $, as a vector space over $ \mathbb{Q} $, can be realized as the cohomology of a space over $ \mathbb{Q} $, and then you can construct a space over $ \mathbb{Z} $, whose cohomology over $ \mathbb{Z} $, after quotienting by torsion, is isomorphic to $ A $.

So E is **always true**, and is the **strongest** that can be said in general.

---

**Conclusion**:
E is the **strongest** that can be said in general, and is **always true**.
